newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Dutch minister sees progress on EU tax competition.
newsitem.headline: Dutch minister sees progress on EU tax competition.

text.p: Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm said on Wednesday he hoped the EU would soon make progress towards eliminating damaging tax competition in the bloc.

The aim, however, was not to impose a single tax on revenue from capital or on corporations, but rather to tackle "unethical taxation being perpetuated", he told the European Parliament economic and monetary affairs committee.
"We don't want a system whereby tax competition will be eliminated altogether...we're talking here about damaging forms," Zalm said.

The Netherlands holds the EU presidency until the end of June. It will hand it over for the second half of 1997 to Luxembourg which has always been a strong opponent of any approximation of tax rates, especially on capital income.
"We hope to make some progress on that before the end of the Dutch presidency," Zalm said.
A group of senior representatives of EU finance ministers will meet again on Friday to try to agree on a code of conduct to avoid harmful tax differences between the Union's partners.

The group has met intensively since March and has identified business taxation as well as the taxation of capital income and withholding taxes on interest and royalties payments between companies as the main points of contention.

Many countries, in particular France, Germany and Belgium, have expressed concern that with the creation of the single currency in 1999 companies will be further encouraged to relocate their operations in lower taxation regions.
Liberated from the exchange rate risk, individuals are also expected to be increasingly tempted to invest their savings in kinder tax environments.
European Commission attempts in the past to achieve some degree of tax harmonisation on savings and other forms of taxation have all failed because decisions require the approval of all EU states.

Luxembourg has always opposed a minimum tax on capital income, but European Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti, who is is in charge of taxation policy, has said he believes progress is possible if the discussion also embraces the sticking point of off-shore centres.
